headline: Southwest Ledge Running Cold and Green — Bass Gone Deep, Bonito Knocking
subhead: The water off the island shifted color this week, and that shift is telling me more than any forecast could.
body_markdown:
I felt it before I saw it. Ran out to the Southwest Ledge before first light Tuesday and the air had that clean, mineral smell it gets when the deep water starts pushing up over the structure — a little cooler on the skin, a little heavier in the lungs. By the time there was enough light to read the surface, I could see why. The water had gone from that flat summer blue to a deep bottle green, streaked with foam lines where the current was working against the rock. That's oxygenated water climbing the ledge, and every August it means the same thing: the biggest bass on this whole stretch of coast have quit chasing bait up top and gone down to live where it's cold and clean.

That's exactly the pattern right now. Surface temps south of the island are sitting in the mid-70s, plenty warm enough to shut the daytime bite down on the flats, but the bass haven't left — they've just gone vertical. I'm finding them in 40 to 60 feet on the Southwest Ledge and out toward the North Rip, holding tight to structure through the day and only really committing to feed on the tide changes, especially the last two hours of a building ebb when the current really starts ripping bait off the edges. Night fishing has been the better call all week. Live eels drifted slow along the rock piles on the Ledge, and bunker chunks fished on a fish-finder rig off the North Rip on the change of tide, have both been producing — not a blitz, but quality fish, the kind that make you check your drag before you set the hook. If you want numbers, fish daytime and expect to work for it. If you want size, fish the dark hours around the tide change and be patient.

Bluefish have been the more reliable daytime story. Bunker schools have been thick off the west side, and wherever those pods bunch up tight against the current, the blues have been putting on a show — real topwater violence, the kind where you can hear it before you see it. We flagged this pattern a few days back, that as long as the high pressure held and the bunker stayed concentrated, you'd get exactly this kind of surface explosion, and that's precisely what's been happening on calm mornings off Grace's Cove and out past Cow Cove. Poppers and metal — Deadly Dicks, half-ounce Kastmasters — thrown right into the boil have been getting hit on nearly every cast when you find the right pod. The trick is timing: get there before the boats pile on and scatter the school.

Fluke have pushed off the shallow flats and settled into deeper water, which is the normal August move. I've had the best luck drifting the channel edges off Great Salt Pond and the drop-offs on the west side in 25 to 35 feet, dragging white Gulp Swimming Mullets on ¾-ounce bucktails, slow and steady along the bottom. It's not been wide open — you're covering water to find the fish holding on structure rather than picking them up everywhere — but the quality has been good, several fish pushing 4 to 5 pounds mixed in with the shorts. Squid strips on a bucktail have also been worth having rigged as a second option; there's a lot of squid around the island right now and the fluke know it.

Scup fishing has been about as good as it gets — an easy, reliable pick if you want dinner without much drama. Anchoring up on the hard bottom off Old Harbor and around the Ledge with squid strips or sandworms on a simple two-hook bottom rig has been filling coolers fast. It's not glamorous fishing, but on a day when the wind's up and the bass bite is tough, it's the play that keeps a trip from being a skunk.

Now, the one everyone's been asking about at the dock — bonito. They're not here yet, not confirmed, but everything about this week says they're close. Surface temps are pushing into that low-to-mid-70s window where they usually show, squid and scup are thick around the island giving them forage to follow in on, and the pattern we've watched build all summer has been marching steadily up the coast — RI breachways and the Vineyard rips first, Block and Montauk right behind. I haven't hooked one yet myself, and I won't tell you I have, but I'd be very surprised if the first fish weren't showing on the south side within the next several days, especially if this stable weather holds. Keep a light spinning rod rigged with Deadly Dicks or small epoxy jigs ready on the boat — you don't want to be digging through a tackle box when the first school shows up busting bait on the surface.

Looking ahead, the tide's rebuilding out of the recent neap phase, which should sharpen up the bite windows across the board — better current on the Ledge and the Rip means a more predictable feed for the bass, and better current generally means tighter, more concentrated bluefish blitzes. If the calm, high-pressure pattern holds through the week, I'd fish the tide changes hard for bass, work the bunker pods early for blues, and keep half an eye on the horizon for that first bonito wake. If a system starts brewing out in the Atlantic, that changes everything fast — this is peak hurricane season, and the island doesn't give you much warning when the weather turns.
